paragraphs: By political jurisdiction I mean the temporary right to pronounce a legal decision that may be given to a political body.

Under absolute governments, extraordinary forms of procedure would serve no purpose. The prince in whose name an offender is prosecuted is as much the sovereign of the courts as of everything else, and the way people think of his power is security enough. His only fear is that the outward formalities of justice may be neglected, and that his authority may be dishonored from a wish to make it more absolute. But in most free countries, where the majority can never influence the courts as an absolute monarch does, judicial power has sometimes been placed for a time in the representatives of the nation. People have judged it better to confuse the functions of the different authorities for a while than to violate the necessary principle that government is one.

England, France, and the United States have established this political jurisdiction by law, and it is interesting to see how differently these three great nations have applied the principle. In England and in France the House of Lords and the Chambre des Pairs *a form the highest criminal court of their respective nations. Although they do not habitually try all political offenses, they are competent to try them all. Another political body has the right of impeachment before the House of Lords. The only difference between the two countries in this respect is that in England the Commons may impeach whomever they please before the Lords, whereas in France the Deputies can use this mode of prosecution only against the ministers of the Crown.
a [ [As it existed under the constitutional monarchy until 1848.]]
In both countries the upper house may use all the existing penal laws of the nation to punish the offenders.

In the United States, as in Europe, one branch of the legislature has the power to impeach and another to judge. The House of Representatives accuses the offender, and the Senate decides his sentence. But the Senate may try only the people the House of Representatives sends to it, and these must be public officials. The Senate’s jurisdiction is therefore narrower than that of the Peers of France, while the Representatives’ right of impeachment is broader than the Deputies’. The great difference between Europe and America, however, is this. In Europe political tribunals may apply every provision of the penal code. In America, once they have removed the offender from his official rank and declared him unfit to hold any political office in the future, their jurisdiction ends and the ordinary tribunals take over.

Suppose, for instance, that the President of the United States has committed the crime of high treason. The House of Representatives impeaches him and the Senate removes him from office; he must then be tried by a jury, which alone can deprive him of his liberty or his life. This illustrates the subject we are treating exactly. The political jurisdiction established by the laws of Europe is intended to try great offenders, whatever their birth, their rank, or their power in the State, and to this end all the privileges of the courts of justice are temporarily extended to a great political assembly. The legislator is then transformed into a magistrate. He is called on to admit, to distinguish, and to punish the offense, and because he exercises all the authority of a judge, the law binds him to observe all the duties of that high office and all the formalities of justice. When a public official is impeached before an English or a French political tribunal and found guilty, the sentence deprives him ipso facto of his functions, and it may declare him incapable of resuming them or any others in the future. But in this case the political interdict is a consequence of the sentence and not the sentence itself. In Europe the sentence of a political tribunal is to be regarded as a judicial verdict rather than as an administrative measure. In the United States the opposite is true. The decision of the Senate is judicial in form, since the senators must follow the practices and formalities of a court of justice. It is judicial in the motives it rests on, since the Senate is in general obliged to take an offense at common law as the basis of its sentence. Nevertheless the object of the proceeding is purely administrative. Had the American legislator intended to invest a political body with great judicial authority, its action would not have been limited to the circle of public officials, since the most dangerous enemies of the State may hold no office at all. This is especially true in republics, where party influence is the first of authorities and where many a leader’s strength is increased by his holding no legal power.

Suppose the American legislator had meant to give society a way of repressing offenses against the State by exemplary punishment, as ordinary justice does. Then he would have put every resource of the penal code at the disposal of the political tribunals. But the weapon they hold is imperfect. It can never reach the most dangerous offenders, because men who aim at the total overthrow of the laws are not likely to complain of a political interdict.

The main object of the political jurisdiction that exists in the United States is therefore to deprive the ill-disposed citizen of an authority he has misused and to prevent him from ever acquiring it again. This is plainly an administrative measure sanctioned by the formalities of a judicial decision. In this matter the Americans have created a mixed system. They have surrounded the act that removes a public official with the safeguards of a political trial, and they have taken from all political condemnations their severest penalties. Every link of the system can easily be traced from this point. We see at once why the American constitutions subject all civil officials to the jurisdiction of the Senate, while the military, whose crimes are nevertheless more formidable, are exempt from that tribunal. In the civil service none of the American officials can be said to be removable: the offices some of them hold cannot be taken from them, and the others are chosen for a term that cannot be shortened. It is therefore necessary to try them all in order to deprive them of their authority. But military officers depend on the chief magistrate of the State, who is himself a civil official, and the decision that condemns him is a blow to them all.

If we now compare the American and the European systems, we find differences just as striking in the different effects each of them produces or may produce. In France and in England the jurisdiction of political bodies is looked on as an extraordinary resource, to be used only to rescue society from unusual dangers. It cannot be denied that these tribunals, as they are constituted in Europe, tend to violate the conservative principle of the balance of power in the State and to threaten the lives and liberties of the subject incessantly. The same political jurisdiction in the United States is only indirectly hostile to the balance of power. It cannot menace the lives of the citizens, and it does not hover over the community as it does in Europe, since only those who submitted to its authority by accepting office are exposed to the severity of its investigations. It is at the same time less formidable and less effective. Indeed, the legislators of the United States have not considered it a remedy for the more violent evils of society, but an ordinary means of conducting the government. In this respect it probably exercises more real influence on the social body in America than in Europe. We must not be misled by the apparent mildness of American legislation on everything relating to political jurisdiction. It should be observed, first, that in the United States the tribunal that passes sentence is made up of the same elements, and subject to the same influences, as the body that impeaches the offender. This uniformity gives an almost irresistible impulse to the vindictive passions of parties. If political judges in the United States cannot inflict such heavy penalties as those of Europe, there is the less chance that they will acquit a prisoner. The conviction, if less formidable, is more certain. The principal object of the political tribunals of Europe is to punish the offender; the purpose of those in America is to deprive him of his authority. A political condemnation in the United States may therefore be regarded as a preventive measure, and there is no reason to restrict the judges to the exact definitions of criminal law. Nothing is more alarming than the excessive latitude with which political offenses are described in the laws of America. Article II, Section 4, of the Constitution of the United States runs thus: “The President, Vice-President, and all civil officers of the United States shall be removed from office on impeachment for, and conviction of, treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.” Many of the State constitutions are even less explicit. “Public officers,” says the Constitution of Massachusetts, *b “shall be impeached for misconduct or maladministration”; the Constitution of Virginia declares that all civil officers who have offended against the State by maladministration, corruption, or other high crimes may be impeached by the House of Delegates; and in some constitutions no offenses are specified, so as to subject public officials to unlimited responsibility. *c But I will venture to affirm that it is precisely their mildness that makes the American laws most formidable in this respect. We have shown that in Europe the removal of an official and his political interdiction are consequences of the penalty he is to undergo, and that in America they constitute the penalty itself. The result is that in Europe political tribunals are invested with rights they are afraid to use, and the fear of punishing too much keeps them from punishing at all. But in America no one hesitates to inflict a penalty from which humanity does not recoil. To condemn a political opponent to death in order to deprive him of his power is to commit what all the world would execrate as a horrible assassination. But to declare that opponent unworthy to exercise that authority, to deprive him of it, and to leave him uninjured in life and limb may be judged the fair outcome of the struggle. Yet this sentence, so easy to pronounce, is fatally severe for most of those on whom it falls. Great criminals may undoubtedly defy its intangible rigor, but ordinary offenders will dread it as a condemnation that destroys their position in the world, casts a blight on their honor, and condemns them to a shameful inactivity worse than death. The influence that the jurisdiction of political bodies exercises in the United States on the progress of society may not appear formidable, but it is only the more immense for that. It does not directly coerce the subject, but it makes the majority more absolute over those in power. It does not confer unbounded authority on the legislator, to be exerted at some momentous crisis, but it establishes a temperate and regular influence, available at all times. If the power is reduced, it can on the other hand be used more conveniently and abused more easily. By preventing political tribunals from inflicting judicial punishments, the Americans seem to have escaped the worst consequences of legislative tyranny, rather than tyranny itself. And I am not sure that political jurisdiction, as it is constituted in the United States, is not the most formidable weapon ever placed in the rude grasp of a popular majority. When the American republics begin to degenerate, it will be easy to verify the truth of this observation by noting whether the number of political impeachments increases. *d
